newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian wheat exports halt on domestic pressures.
newsitem.headline: Indian wheat exports halt on domestic pressures.

text.p: India has halted wheat exports to curb rising domestic prices and augument supplies, traders and analysts said on Wednesday.
Traders said there had been no wheat exports since September 30 as the state-owned Agricultural and Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA) had not issued export licences.
Earlier this year the government released 1.13 million tonnes of wheat for export in fiscal 1996/97 (April-March).

"The reasons are political. It is just to control domestic prices by ensuring ample supplies," said an official with a leading Delhi-based export company. He said foodgrain stocks, though depleted, were sufficient to allow exports.
An APEDA official said so far there had been no government directive to issue licences for wheat exports. "We might get some information next week," the official told Reuters.
The government early this month put a ceiling of 150,000 tonnes on wheat product exports in fiscal 1996/97 (April-March). Wheat products were earlier exported freely.
Analysts said the state-run Food Corporation of India (FCI) had procured only 8.15 million tonnes of wheat from farmers in fiscal 1995/96 against a target of 12 million tonnes.
They said farmers preferred to sell wheat in the open market at 550 rupees per quintal, rather than to FCI, which bought it at only about 380 rupees per quintal.
They said ample wheat was available in the market though FCI had procured less this year. "What the government has done is a knee-jerk reaction," one analyst said.
Last year the government released 2.5 million tonnes of wheat for export in fiscal 1995/96. But Indian exporters were unable to ship it all by March 31, the end of the fiscal year.
Under pressure from exporters complaining about congested ports, the government extended the deadline to September 30.

"The reason for their banning exports is an increase in inflation levels and a rise in domestic wheat prices," said S. M. Virmani, an official of the Hyderabad-based International Crop Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics.
Domestic wheat prices have been pushing higher over the last few months. Wheat prices rose by an average 20 percent compared to the prices in the same period last year.
"If they allow more exports there could be panic and government is being cautious," Virmani said.

One analyst said some foreign buyers were cancelling contracts since international wheat prices had dropped $20 per tonne in the last two months. Some exporters were unable to meet their commitments due to a rise in domestic wheat prices.
He said India's wheat output in 1995/96 (April-March) was estimated at 62.6 million tonnes compared with 65.2 million in 1994/95. But it was too early to estimate next year's crop.
